intro: You have arrived at Dascylium, an ancient city in Balıkesir province, whose story runs from the 8th century BC to the 4th century BC. This Mysian city was the seat of the Persian satraps in Anatolia, and it is famous for its sculpted stonework.
history: From the 8th century BC this place passed from hand to hand: Phrygian, then Lydian, then Persian. After Cyrus the Great conquered Anatolia, it became the seat of the satrapy of Hellespontine Phrygia, home to a palace of the Persian nobility. Then the city was lost from view, until it was rediscovered in 1952.
structure-1: You are now at the Persian Palace, a palace building dating to the period of Persian rule. Pause for a moment and imagine the court of the Persian nobility gathered here.
structure-2: Here is the Rock Altar, an altar carved straight into a sacred rock. Stand still for a moment: this was a place where people came to honour the sacred.
structure-3: Now look for the North Tower, the defensive tower on the northern side of the city. From here, the city's defenders kept watch.
structure-4: These are the remains of the Phrygian Settlement, dating to the Phrygian period, one of the earliest chapters in this site's long story.
structure-5: Here are the Terrace Buildings, erected on sloping ground and held in place by retaining terraces. The builders turned a difficult slope into usable ground.
facts: Did you know? The Persian reliefs of Dascylium are among the most important examples of Achaemenid art found in Anatolia. This was the seat of the Persian satrapy of western Anatolia, the best-documented site of Persian rule in the region. Hundreds of clay sealings survive: all that is left of an archive that burned, preserved because the fire baked them. And the mound overlooks Lake Manyas; ancient sources describe the satrap's garden here as a hunting park.
outro: This brings our tour of Dascylium to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These stones have waited for centuries; let them keep waiting for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
